devices.description: Casa C100G CMTS/CCAP - 13RU, 14 paired front/rear slots. Front and rear slot N are two halves of one logical position: a DOCSIS line card in front N requires its I/O partner in rear N.

gaps.note: The BDM2/BDM2m datasheet states "Total Power 300 W" in a technical specifications table headed "BDM2/2 m with 6+12 IO Card", whose RF connector row describes that card's six downstream and twelve upstream ports. The figure is the assembly's. A BDM position is TWO modules here - casa/bdm in a front bay and casa/io-6p12 in the paired rear bay, which is why casa/bdm already carries `pairs-with` - and no document we hold divides the 300 W between them. Writing it onto the front module would make the chassis total come out right and the answer to "what does a BDM front module draw" come out wrong, so neither half carries a figure and the chassis total stays a floor. The arithmetic does not settle it either way: 12 x 300 W lands on the C100G's stated 3.6 kW whether the 300 W is the pair or the front half with small rear cards. The C100G HIG corroborates the assembly reading and hedges it: Tables A-10 and A-11 both read "Approximately 300W per BDM" under titles scoping them to the BDM WITH its 6+12 I/O. THE LIBRARY IS CURRENTLY INCONSISTENT ABOUT THIS, ON PURPOSE AND VISIBLY. The three BDM variants carry NO power figure, for the reason above. The DQM and DCU cards added later DO carry one - DS8x8 220, DS8x96 320, DS8x192 350, US16x8 220, US16x4 150 - each with a `power-scope` provenance entry saying in the vendor's own words that the number covers the card WITH its I/O module and must not have a rear figure added to it. Both are defensible readings of the same problem: one keeps the per-module answer honest and the chassis total a floor, the other keeps the vendor's only published number reachable. They should not stay different once a pairing-scoped mechanism exists, and this is the record of which way each went and why, so that whoever unifies them is not guessing. THE THREE REAR RF I/O CARDS ADDED LATER FALL ON THE SAME SIDE OF THIS AS THE 6+12. casa/rfd, casa/rfu-16x8 and casa/ups-32x4 carry NO power figure, because Tables A-8 and A-9 give their port counts and connector types and no watts at all, and every figure Casa does publish for the slot is already the pair's - Table A-3 heads the DQM column "Maximum consumption with I/O module" and Table A-4 gives "Single DCU w/ RFU I/O" 200 W against "Single DCU w/ RFU UPS 32x4 I/O" 220 W for the same US16x8. Subtracting one from the other to get a rear card's share would be our arithmetic and would also be the wrong subtraction - the 20 W is the difference between two PAIRINGS, not between two I/O cards.
gaps.wanted: a pairable unit that can carry properties, so that a figure measured on a pair can be attached to the pair. The scope is now DATA - every card here declares `power-draw-scope: module-with-paired-io`, so a chassis sum knows not to add the rear partner and L30 catches it if one gains its own figure - but the scope says only THAT the figure covers a pair, not WHICH pair. The C100G HIG gives the same US16x8 200 W with the RFU I/O and 220 W with the RFU UPS 32x4, and the manifest can carry only one of them. Asking for "a per-module figure" was the wrong question: Casa states none, and one may not exist to be divided out. What is missing is the mechanism, and enough vendors doing this to design one from - Casa is the only one in the corpus.

gaps.note: The HIG body text states "Each fan assembly module has a maximum power consumption of 100W, totaling 300W across the three fan assemblies". Table A-2 of the same guide gives the row "Fan assembly (3)" as "330W maximum, 220W typical". Both are about the set of three and 300 is not 330. The contract takes 100 W because it is the only figure stated PER MODULE, which is the granularity a bay occupant needs; dividing 330 by three would be our arithmetic, not the vendor's. A chassis total is therefore 30 W light against the guide's own set figure, and no per-module typical exists at all.
gaps.wanted: a measurement from a running chassis, a vendor erratum, or a later revision of the guide that drops one of the two figures

gaps.note: Casa rates a power ENTRY module in amps and volts, never in watts. Table A-1 gives "Voltage -42 to -60VDC" and "Current 20A nominal per feed", and the chassis nameplate at Figure 1-3 gives "-48VDC, 30A per Feed (4+4 Feeds)" - but no document states a wattage, and deriving one means choosing a point the vendor left open: two current figures across a voltage range put V x I anywhere from about 810 W to 1800 W per feed. gaps.note: Casa says two things about this terminal and they do not agree. The prose in "Connecting the chassis to ground" says it "provides two M6 screws to connect a double-lug ground terminal cable". Figures 1-2 and 1-4 both DRAW three studs, in a 2x2 grid with the protective-earth mark in the fourth corner, and the two figures agree with each other. THE DRAWING IS FOLLOWED, and the model carries three. The figure is the only source that says anything about arrangement at all, so following the prose would mean inventing a layout for the two it describes; and a third stud has easy explanations - a spare, an alternate lug pitch - while a stud drawn twice that is not there has none. That is a judgement, not a reading, which is why it is filed here. THE PITCH IS NOT MEASURED FROM EITHER. It is borrowed from casa/ground-bolts@1, 15.3, off Jason`s hand-built C100G rear SVG. Figure 1-4 gives 13.2 across and 14.7 down for what must be one square grid - an 11 percent disagreement with itself, which is that figure`s anisotropy rather than a rectangular pattern.
gaps.wanted: a photograph of the C40G rear lower-left corner, which would settle the count and the pitch together in one look

gaps.note: The card band runs 37.5 to 386.7 in a body 432.95 wide, so it sits 37.5 from the left edge and 46.25 from the right - 8.75 mm out of centre, or 4.375 on the band's own centreline. Everything inside the band agrees with everything else; the question is whether the band is really off-centre in the metal, and nothing we hold answers it. IT IS NOT COSMETIC, and the AC input panel is where it bites. Its four C14 inlets sit behind the four front power supplies. Reflect the supply centres about the PANEL and the inlets are 1.2 out; reflect them about the CHASSIS - which is what walking round a box actually does - and they are 9.95 out. The gap between those two answers IS this asymmetry, and no arrangement of the parts inside the band can close it, because the disagreement is between the band and the chassis rather than within either. THE SUPPORTING NUMBERS ARE ALSO ODD IN THE SAME DIRECTION. The two front fan strips measure 36.0 wide each - equal, as you would expect - but leave 1.5 outside them on the left and 10.25 on the right. Two equal strips with unequal surrounds is exactly the shape of a band that has been positioned from one edge. NOT RESOLVED BY GUESSING, deliberately. Re-centring the band would move the two fan strips, the card bays on both faces, the PSU row, the PSU cover and the AC panel - and it would be one estimate reconciled against another, which this device's `pem-band-top-edge` note already records going wrong twice in opposite directions.
gaps.wanted: a dimensioned C40G front or rear elevation from Casa, or a tape measure across a real chassis from its left edge to the first card slot and from the last card slot to its right edge

gaps.note: The PEM band's BOTTOM edge at 264.5 is agreed by every source and is not in doubt. Its TOP edge is known only to about 2 mm, and the three candidates each have support: 194.0 is the direct reading of Figure 1-4 and is impossible, because the card slot above ends at 194.82; 194.82 is flush against that slot; 196.0 is what the bays carry and is what the manifest now uses, on the argument that 194.82 is an accumulation of six DERIVED slot pitches (426.6 mm over 14 slots on the C100G, carried across) and that the front face shows a measured 1.48 mm margin in the equivalent position. That argument is sound but it is an argument, not a measurement, and the whole disagreement is six pixels at 2.982 px/mm. A tape measure on a real C40G, or any Casa drawing that dimensions the rear panel, would settle it in one number. FIGURE 1-12 HAS NOW BEEN LOOKED AT AND DOES NOT SETTLE IT, recorded so nobody spends the search twice. "C40G power entry module" is the only isolated drawing of this part and the first independent look anything has had at it. Its body measures 866 x 381 px for an aspect of 2.273. The modelled 158.0 x 68.5 is 2.307 and the superseded 158.0 x 70.5 is 2.241, and 2.273 lands 0.04 percent off the midpoint of those two - at 158.0 wide it implies a height of 69.51. IT IS EQUIDISTANT AND CONFIRMS NEITHER. This guide's isolated part drawings are in any case demonstrably about 10 percent wrong about their own aspect - Figure 1-20 draws a card at 12.54 whose real aspect is 11.34 - so a 1.5 percent lean is well inside the drawing's own error. THE NUMBER IS THEREFORE NOT MOVED. It has been moved twice already, in both directions, and a third move on evidence that splits the difference would be the reconciliation loop rather than an escape from it. What Figure 1-12 does confirm is the ARRANGEMENT, which is what a figure is good for: a bolted terminal cover across the top with three fasteners, a minus pair of studs above a plus pair inside two outlined blocks, two release levers standing proud of the body top and bottom, and the yellow disconnect-power label to their right - all of which casa/c40g-pem draws. RECORDED BECAUSE THE MODULE AND THE BAY NOW AGREE, which means nothing will ever flag this again - the fit check that found the original 2 mm discrepancy is satisfied by both being wrong together as easily as by both being right.

devices.description: Cisco ASR 9000 Series ASR 9001 Router - a 2 RU fixed-port aggregation services router with an integrated route processor, four fixed 10 GE SFP+ ports, two modular port adapter bays and 120 Gbps of fabric. Everything is on the front face: both MPA bays, both power supplies, the side-mounted fan tray and every port. The rear is a plain louvred panel.

gaps.note: The ASR 9001-S is the same metal as the ASR 9001 with two of its four fixed SFP+ ports disabled until a licence is applied. That is not a population fact - the cages are physically present and identical - so `bays:` cannot express it, and the ports are correctly drawn present in both configurations. INVESTIGATED AND IT DOES NOT REACH: `component-attrs` is the closest mechanism the format has, and it is keyed by component NAME rather than by placement id. render.py computes `comp_name = ref.split("/")[-1].split("@")[0]` and looks the overrides up by that, so `component-attrs: {sfp-ganged: ...}` would mark all SIX std/sfp-ganged instances on this chassis - both CLUSTER ports and all four SFP+ - when only two are disabled. A placement can carry `attrs:` per instance but not per configuration; `component-attrs` is per configuration but not per instance. The 9001-S needs both at once and neither mechanism spans the gap. The same edge stops this configuration carrying its own 60 Gbps fabric figure, since a configuration cannot override device attrs at all.
gaps.wanted: per-instance attrs in a configuration - `component-attrs` keyed by placement id as well as by component name would do it - or a device-attrs override in a configuration. This is a second instance of the shape recorded in working/notes/config-scoped-placements.md, from a different vendor: the format can say what OCCUPIES a bay per configuration, but not what is TRUE of a part per configuration.

gaps.note: Table 4 of the fixed-port install guide gives the 10MHz and 1PPS connectors as DIN 1.0/2.3. The standards registry has no key for it - sma, smb, mcx and f-type are there, DIN 1.0/2.3 is not - so these two openings are declared as panel cutouts at their measured size rather than composed from a std/ part. Substituting sma or smb would name a connector Cisco does not. THE REASON WAS vendor-silent AND THAT WAS THE WRONG TOKEN. Cisco is not silent - it names the connector outright. What is missing is a panel-cutout dimension, which is needs-drawing, and the difference matters because the two tokens ask different things of a reader: vendor-silent reads as closed until better documents appear, needs-drawing reads as an errand somebody can run today. The correction came from asr9k-cards, who had just been wrong in exactly this direction about the XFP - concluding a figure was unsourceable after searching the intake rather than the standards - and found it in INF-8077i ten minutes after looking somewhere else. IEC 61169-8 is the somewhere else here, and nobody has opened it yet.
gaps.wanted: a std/din-1-0-2-3 part and its standards.yaml key. THE CONNECTOR IS STANDARDISED, so a sourced dimension exists to be found rather than estimated - DIN 1.0/2.3 is specified in IEC 61169-8, and any manufacturer's bulkhead-jack panel drawing carries the D-hole figure. std/mcx is the worked example of exactly this being done properly earlier tonight: registered from IEC 61169-36 / CECC 22220 at 4.95 x 4.50 with confidence verified, replacing an estimate that was 28 percent too small. This should be done the same way, and until it is, an sma or smb standing in would be a plausible wrong answer - which is the failure mode this project keeps having to dig back out

devices.description: Cisco ASR 9006 Router - the 10RU, six-slot member of the ASR 9000 Series Aggregation Services Routers. Cards mount HORIZONTALLY: slots 0 and 1 at the bottom of the cage are reserved for a redundant RSP pair, slots 2 to 5 above them take line cards. Two fan trays sit above the cage behind a hinged door, and a single power shelf below it carries the AC or DC power modules, whose inlets are on the rear face. Modelled as a BARE CAGE: every slot is a bay that a card component drops into, not a traced faceplate.

gaps.note: cisco/a9k-pwr-3kw-ac@1 states 142.78 mm wide. Three of them need 428.34 mm and this chassis's power shelf interior measures 416.50, so they do not fit - lint L13 flagged the overlap directly when they were placed at the measured centres. Against that, the stencil's shape box for the 'A9K Power Module' master reads 0.5477 in, which is 139.12 mm at the stencil's 1:10 scale, and my own measurement of the three openings in the ASR 9006 front master gives 138.35, 137.50 and 138.23. Those two agree to under a millimetre, and three at 139.12 come to 417.36 against a 416.50 shelf - the arithmetic a shelf that holds exactly three ought to produce. The 142.78 is most likely the art measured over something that is not the module's seating width, the same class of error as reading a card's shape box instead of its art. The bays here are sized to the measured openings, so the chassis is right and the component and the chassis disagree by about 3.7 mm until someone re-measures the master.
gaps.wanted: a re-measurement of the 'A9K Power Module' stencil master, or a Cisco dimension for the version 1 power module

gaps.note: NINE CARDS SHARE THESE SIX SLOTS AND TWO FAMILIES DISAGREE BY 32.8 mm ON THE ONE AXIS THAT HAS TO FIT ONE OPENING. The line cards and the blank filler are 395.7 mm; all four RSP-880 variants are 428.5. The measured cage opening is 352.59. The line-card story is coherent: a9k-slot-cover's own art measures a PLATE of 362.24 inside a 395.7 envelope, so the plate covers the 352.59 opening with 4.8 mm of overlap per side and the ejector brackets account for the remaining 16.7 per side. Every number has a job. The RSP-880's does not. 428.5 needs 37.96 mm of overlap per side to cover the same opening, and a card centred on this cage reaches x 22.99 to 451.49 in a 444.5 mm chassis - 6.99 mm PAST the outer wall, which is visible in the 3D view as the card's end standing proud of the side of the box. WHERE 428.5 COMES FROM, AND WHY IT IS THE SUSPECT: the RSP-880 data sheet's 'Physical specifications' row. This library's own a9k-rsp880-se provenance already records that NINE RSP AND RP MASTERS IN THE STENCIL ARE ONE DRAWING, scaled to four different stated widths - 402.8, 428.5, 428.2 and 403.4 - so "the drawing is generic across the family and cannot be all four sizes". The cage, by contrast, is measured off this chassis's own master and independently supported by Figure 19. NOT RESOLVED HERE. Two numbers describing different things is the likeliest reading - the same trap as a plate against an envelope - but nothing we hold says WHICH thing 428.5 measures, and inventing a smaller one would be the reconciliation this project keeps digging back out.
gaps.wanted: a Cisco mechanical drawing of an RSP-880 faceplate, or one measurement across a real card from ejector tip to ejector tip. Either settles it for all four variants at once and for every chassis they go in. REQUESTED FROM THE LAB, 2026-08-26, and tracked as roc-ops/ndv#16 - that issue carries the three conflicting Cisco figures and what to do when the number arrives.

gaps.note: NARROWED, not closed. This file and the ASR 9010's carried pitches that disagreed - 46.60 here against 44.33 there - for two chassis that take the same cards. Cisco's RSP-880 sheet resolved the 9010 half: the card is 46.0 mm thick and Cisco names the 9010 among the chassis it serves, so a 44.33 slot is impossible there and that cage is now divided on published card thicknesses. THIS CHASSIS IS NOT DISCRIMINATED BY THAT EVIDENCE. Its 279.63 mm cage admits both readings: four line card slots at 41.4 plus two RSP slots at 46.0 is 257.6, leaving 22.03 for guides; and an even six-way division at 46.60 is also >= 46.0 and so also admits the RSP-880. The even division is kept because it is what the cage measures and because nothing here favours the other, but it is an assumption and the 9010 shows the family does not always divide evenly. Neither this master nor the 9010's prints slot labels or draws cage dividers, which is why both were assumptions in the first place - the 9904, 9906, 9910, 9912 and 9922 all have a ruler in the picture and these two do not.
gaps.wanted: a dimensioned front elevation of the ASR 9006, or a per-slot width from any Cisco document

gaps.note: Two figures in b-asr9k-overview-reference-guide.pdf give the ASR 9006 body width differently. Table 13 "Cisco ASR 9000 Series Routers Physical Descriptions" (p130) says 17.50 inches (44.45 cm). devices.description: Cisco ASR 9010 Router - the 21RU, ten-slot member of the ASR 9000 Series Aggregation Services Routers. Cards mount VERTICALLY across the full width of the cage: the two CENTRE slots, 4 and 5, are reserved for a redundant RSP pair, with four line card slots either side of them. A cable management tray runs along the top, two stacked fan trays and a front air intake sit below the cage, and two power shelves fill the bottom. Modelled as a BARE CAGE: every slot is a bay a card component drops into, not a traced faceplate.

gaps.note: THESE BAY DIMENSIONS WERE GROWN TO MEET A COMPONENT AND ARE NOT MEASUREMENTS. Each was set by taking the size of a card the bay accepts, because a fit check reported the bay as too small. On this chassis: 403.10 on 8 bays - the 5th-generation envelope, 403.10 long 406.40 on 2 bays - a9k-rsp, 406.40 long The danger is specific and it is why they are listed rather than left to look like geometry. A fit check compares a bay to a component and NEITHER of them to the world, so it is satisfied by both being wrong together exactly as easily as by both being right. Every mismatch resolved by moving one side removes the signal without adding any truth, and once resolved nothing will flag it again. These are the entries where that happened, so the record survives the check going quiet. What IS independently grounded and is not in this list: the cage extents, measured off the stencil and confirmed on several chassis by printed slot labels or a card guide rail; the slot pitch; the 395.70 fourth-generation envelope, which is Cisco's own "includes ejector bracket/lever" figure; and the shapesheet sizes for the power modules and fan trays. The ejector arithmetic that explains why a bay legitimately exceeds its cage opening - 355.60 against 395.70, 40.10 mm - is also sourced, and it justifies the SHAPE of these numbers without justifying any particular one of them.
gaps.wanted: a dimensioned figure giving the clear opening of any ASR 9000 card cage, which would replace every reconciled figure above with a measured one

gaps.note: A THIRD LINE OF EVIDENCE ON THE ~428 mm CONTROL CARDS, derived rather than asserted, and it comes from parts that have nothing to do with the question. The vertical space available to a card is bounded by whatever structure sits above and below its cage, and on this chassis that space measures the figure recorded in card-envelope-headroom below. A card envelope larger than that cannot be installed whatever any data sheet says, because something else is already there. Applied across the family: ASR 9010 399.96 mm between the cable management tray and the card guide bar ASR 9910 421.79 mm between the tray band and the front air intake ASR 9922 420.30 mm between the tray band and the fan band ASR 9912 439.21 mm - does NOT exclude 428.5, so this chassis is silent on the question ASR 9906 unbounded above in the model, so no constraint is derivable Three of the five independently exclude a 428.2-428.5 card. That is a separate argument from the slot pitch and from the ejector arithmetic, and it agrees with both. THE 9912 DOES NOT EXCLUDE IT and is recorded as silent rather than as agreement - a constraint that fails to bite is not evidence either way, and reporting it as if it were would manufacture support. The 9010's 399.96 also sits 3.14 mm under the 403.10 fifth-generation envelope its bays now carry, which is a smaller open question of the same kind.
gaps.wanted: a figure dimensioning the clear vertical opening of any ASR 9000 card cage, which would turn all of this from derived to measured

gaps.note: THE SECOND AXIS OF THE SAME CONFLICT, and it makes the first one much harder to explain away. The RSP-880 family is published at 428.5 mm on its long axis. Two Cisco statements fix what a line card measures on that axis in this family: Table A-10 of OL-17500-09 gives the original-generation card 14 in (355.60 mm) with NO qualifier, and the 4th-generation data sheets give 15.58 in (395.70) explicitly "including ejector bracket/lever". The 40.10 mm between them is the ejectors, about 20 mm each end - which is also why a bay declared at the 395.70 envelope is legitimately longer than the cage opening it sits in. Against that, 428.50 does not reconcile. Subtract the same 40.10 of ejector and the plate would still be 33.45 mm longer than this chassis's measured cage - a cage independently confirmed to 0.65 mm by Table A-10's own 355.60. So BOTH published RSP-880 dimensions, 46.0 thick and 428.5 long, are irreconcilable with a cage that two unrelated sources agree on. That is why the bays were NOT inflated to hold it. Building five chassis around a pair of numbers that contradict the only independently confirmed dimension in the family would put the error into the geometry instead of into the record. The accepts keep the RSP-880 where Cisco names it; the bays stay at what the cage and the reconcilable envelopes allow.
gaps.wanted: the RSP-880's plate dimensions as distinct from whatever 46.0 x 428.5 measures, or a photograph of an RSP-880 beside a line card

gaps.note: Cisco's RSP-880 and RSP880-LT data sheet gives "Height: 1.81 in. (4.60 cm)", i.e. 46.0 mm, and names the ASR 9006, 9010, 9904, 9906 and 9910 as the chassis they are the system processor for. THAT WIDTH EXCEEDS THE MEASURED SLOT PITCH ON EVERY CHASSIS IN THE FAMILY: 9010 44.33 9906 43.42 9910 43.78 9912 44.06 9922 44.06 and three of those pitches are measured from PRINTED SLOT LABELS or a card guide rail with a spread of 0.11 to 0.20 mm - among the best-supported numbers in this library. A card cannot be thicker than its slot, so 1.81 in is not the seating width; it is most likely taken over the ejector levers, the same way Cisco's line card "Width" is stated as "includes ejector bracket/lever" elsewhere. The accepts lists keep the RSP-880 family where Cisco names it, because a compatibility claim is Cisco's to make. The bays are sized to what the measured opening can hold. So a reader will find a bay narrower than a component it accepts, and that is a RECORDED CONFLICT between two sources rather than an oversight - the alternative was to inflate five chassis' geometry to fit one published number that three independent pitch measurements contradict.
gaps.wanted: the RSP-880's seating width as distinct from its over-ejector width, or any Cisco statement of an ASR 9000 slot pitch

gaps.note: cisco/a9k-pwr-3kw-ac@1 states 142.78 mm wide. Three of them need 428.34 mm and this chassis's power shelf interior measures 416.50, so they do not fit - lint L13 flagged the overlap directly when they were placed at the measured centres. Against that, the stencil's shape box for the 'A9K Power Module' master reads 0.5477 in, which is 139.12 mm at the stencil's 1:10 scale, and my own measurement of the three openings in the ASR 9006 front master gives 138.35, 137.50 and 138.23. Those two agree to under a millimetre, and three at 139.12 come to 417.36 against a 416.50 shelf - the arithmetic a shelf that holds exactly three ought to produce. The 142.78 is most likely the art measured over something that is not the module's seating width, the same class of error as reading a card's shape box instead of its art. The bays here are sized to the measured openings, so the chassis is right and the component and the chassis disagree by about 3.7 mm until someone re-measures the master.
gaps.wanted: a re-measurement of the 'A9K Power Module' stencil master, or a Cisco dimension for the version 1 power module

gaps.note: The two RSP slots are 46.0 mm because that is the RSP-880's published thickness and Cisco names this chassis as one it serves - so 46.0 is a LOWER BOUND on the slot, not a measurement of it. The eight line card slots are 41.4 on the same basis. The 20.12 mm those twenty-two millimetres of card leave over is distributed as eleven equal guides, which is arithmetic rather than observation: the real chassis may well have wider guides between the cages and narrower ones within them. What IS solid is that an even ten-way division is impossible, since 44.33 is thinner than a card Cisco says seats here. Searched and not found: any per-slot width in the Ethernet Line Card Installation Guide, the Hardware Installation Guide or the Overview and Reference Guide, and the stencil master draws the cage as a single undivided rectangle.

gaps.note: The ASR 9010's two fan trays occupy the band between the card guide bar at 566.51 mm and the front air intake grille at 673.60 mm - 107.09 mm for the pair, which is measured and solid. devices.description: Cisco ASR 9922 Router - 44 RU and the largest of the family. TWENTY vertical line card slots in two cages, one above and one below a central cage of two route processors flanking seven fabric cards, with four fan trays between the cages and four power shelves across the top. The line cards in the LOWER cage, slots 10 to 19, are installed UPSIDE DOWN. Modelled as a bare cage.

gaps.note: THESE BAY DIMENSIONS WERE GROWN TO MEET A COMPONENT AND ARE NOT MEASUREMENTS. Each was set by taking the size of a card the bay accepts, because a fit check reported the bay as too small. On this chassis: 42.67 on 20 bays - a9k-4hg-flex, 42.67 thick 403.10 on 20 bays - the 5th-generation envelope, 403.10 long The danger is specific and it is why they are listed rather than left to look like geometry. A fit check compares a bay to a component and NEITHER of them to the world, so it is satisfied by both being wrong together exactly as easily as by both being right. Every mismatch resolved by moving one side removes the signal without adding any truth, and once resolved nothing will flag it again. These are the entries where that happened, so the record survives the check going quiet. What IS independently grounded and is not in this list: the cage extents, measured off the stencil and confirmed on several chassis by printed slot labels or a card guide rail; the slot pitch; the 395.70 fourth-generation envelope, which is Cisco's own "includes ejector bracket/lever" figure; and the shapesheet sizes for the power modules and fan trays. The ejector arithmetic that explains why a bay legitimately exceeds its cage opening - 355.60 against 395.70, 40.10 mm - is also sourced, and it justifies the SHAPE of these numbers without justifying any particular one of them.
gaps.wanted: a dimensioned figure giving the clear opening of any ASR 9000 card cage, which would replace every reconciled figure above with a measured one

gaps.note: A THIRD LINE OF EVIDENCE ON THE ~428 mm CONTROL CARDS, derived rather than asserted, and it comes from parts that have nothing to do with the question. The vertical space available to a card is bounded by whatever structure sits above and below its cage, and on this chassis that space measures the figure recorded in card-envelope-headroom below. A card envelope larger than that cannot be installed whatever any data sheet says, because something else is already there. Applied across the family: ASR 9010 399.96 mm between the cable management tray and the card guide bar ASR 9910 421.79 mm between the tray band and the front air intake ASR 9922 420.30 mm between the tray band and the fan band ASR 9912 439.21 mm - does NOT exclude 428.5, so this chassis is silent on the question ASR 9906 unbounded above in the model, so no constraint is derivable Three of the five independently exclude a 428.2-428.5 card. That is a separate argument from the slot pitch and from the ejector arithmetic, and it agrees with both. THE 9912 DOES NOT EXCLUDE IT and is recorded as silent rather than as agreement - a constraint that fails to bite is not evidence either way, and reporting it as if it were would manufacture support. The 9010's 399.96 also sits 3.14 mm under the 403.10 fifth-generation envelope its bays now carry, which is a smaller open question of the same kind.
gaps.wanted: a figure dimensioning the clear vertical opening of any ASR 9000 card cage, which would turn all of this from derived to measured

gaps.note: THE SECOND AXIS OF THE SAME CONFLICT, and it makes the first one much harder to explain away. The RSP-880 family is published at 428.5 mm on its long axis. Two Cisco statements fix what a line card measures on that axis in this family: Table A-10 of OL-17500-09 gives the original-generation card 14 in (355.60 mm) with NO qualifier, and the 4th-generation data sheets give 15.58 in (395.70) explicitly "including ejector bracket/lever". The 40.10 mm between them is the ejectors, about 20 mm each end - which is also why a bay declared at the 395.70 envelope is legitimately longer than the cage opening it sits in. Against that, 428.50 does not reconcile. Subtract the same 40.10 of ejector and the plate would still be 33.45 mm longer than this chassis's measured cage - a cage independently confirmed to 0.65 mm by Table A-10's own 355.60. So BOTH published RSP-880 dimensions, 46.0 thick and 428.5 long, are irreconcilable with a cage that two unrelated sources agree on. That is why the bays were NOT inflated to hold it. Building five chassis around a pair of numbers that contradict the only independently confirmed dimension in the family would put the error into the geometry instead of into the record. The accepts keep the RSP-880 where Cisco names it; the bays stay at what the cage and the reconcilable envelopes allow.
gaps.wanted: the RSP-880's plate dimensions as distinct from whatever 46.0 x 428.5 measures, or a photograph of an RSP-880 beside a line card

gaps.note: Cisco's RSP-880 and RSP880-LT data sheet gives "Height: 1.81 in. (4.60 cm)", i.e. 46.0 mm, and names the ASR 9006, 9010, 9904, 9906 and 9910 as the chassis they are the system processor for. THAT WIDTH EXCEEDS THE MEASURED SLOT PITCH ON EVERY CHASSIS IN THE FAMILY: 9010 44.33 9906 43.42 9910 43.78 9912 44.06 9922 44.06 and three of those pitches are measured from PRINTED SLOT LABELS or a card guide rail with a spread of 0.11 to 0.20 mm - among the best-supported numbers in this library. A card cannot be thicker than its slot, so 1.81 in is not the seating width; it is most likely taken over the ejector levers, the same way Cisco's line card "Width" is stated as "includes ejector bracket/lever" elsewhere. The accepts lists keep the RSP-880 family where Cisco names it, because a compatibility claim is Cisco's to make. The bays are sized to what the measured opening can hold. So a reader will find a bay narrower than a component it accepts, and that is a RECORDED CONFLICT between two sources rather than an oversight - the alternative was to inflate five chassis' geometry to fit one published number that three independent pitch measurements contradict.
gaps.wanted: the RSP-880's seating width as distinct from its over-ejector width, or any Cisco statement of an ASR 9000 slot pitch

gaps.note: The guide states that "line cards must be installed upside down in slots 10 through 19 of the bottom card cage, whereas in slots 0 though 9 of the top card cage, the line cards are installed right side up". This is a real property of the chassis and the model cannot currently express it. The bays for 10 to 19 are geometrically identical to 0 to 9 and carry no rotation, because the card is inverted about its own long axis rather than rotated in the plane of the panel - a `rotate: 180` would spin the faceplate end for end, which is a different thing and would put the ejectors at the wrong ends. So a card rendered in slot 15 will show its ports and its part number the same way up as one in slot 5, and on real hardware it would not. Anyone reading port positions off the lower cage should know that.
gaps.wanted: a mirror or flip transform on a bay, distinct from rotation, or a photograph settling exactly which way an inverted card reads

gaps.note: RP0 and RP1 are CUTOUTS rather than bays. The candidate component is cisco/asr-9922-rp-se/-tr, named for this chassis and carrying Table 23's "RP Card" figure of 259 W, but it declares a slot envelope of 46.0 mm and this cage's nine positions divide its measured 429.04 mm span into 47.67 mm each - which the RP would fit - while the LINE CARD cages divide into 43.388 and the rail pitch is 44.06. A 46.0 mm supervisor does not fit a 44 mm slot, and the same 46.0 x 428.5 x 628.9 appears on a9k-rsp880-se/-tr, byte for byte, which suggests one derivation reused rather than two measurements. Until that width is re-derived from the shapesheet these two positions stay openings. The seven fabric positions beside them ARE bays, because a99-sfc3's 41.4 fits comfortably.
gaps.wanted: a re-derivation of asr-9922-rp's width from the stencil shapesheet, both axes from one source

gaps.note: The four fan trays are cutouts. cisco/asr-9922-fan-v3 declares 475.96 mm wide and this chassis's BODY is 447.0, so the component is 29 mm wider than the box it goes in. Compare cisco/asr-9910-fan at 445.2, which sits inside its own 447 mm body correctly. Both are class cooling and one of them is measured against the rack face rather than the body - the stencil records rack-face widths for trays and covers, and 475.96 is within a few millimetres of the 482.6 mm rack face. The openings here are the measured bands and the component is not placed.
gaps.wanted: asr-9922-fan-v3's width re-derived against the body, or confirmation that the fan tray really does span the rack face and needs a negative offset like a mounting ear

gaps.note: THE BOTTOM IS THE ONLY FACE OF THIS CHASSIS WITH NO SOURCE, and it is not a gap in this file's research. There is no bottom view of ANY ASR 9000 chassis anywhere in the 78-document intake: every figure caption in all 65 PDFs was searched for "Bottom View", "underside" and "bottom of the chassis", and the result is zero hits. That is a fact about how Cisco documents a rack chassis rather than about this model - a face that sits on rack rails and is never serviced gets no figure. The face is SIZED correctly from Table 13, so a rack elevation and the 3D box are the right shape; what it lacks is any statement of what is on it. Nothing is invented to fill it, and no region is added naming the absence, because a check passed by annotating that you have nothing is worse than a check failed honestly. THIS HOLDS THE CHASSIS AT CAPABILITY 2. Front, rear, top, left and right all now carry sourced content; the bottom alone does not, and level 3's implementation requires content on all six. The written design asks only that six faces be "present, sized, and mutually consistent", which this file satisfies - the content requirement comes from `_has_content`, which was written for level 1. See working/notes/deliberately-empty-faces.md.
gaps.wanted: a bottom elevation, a photograph of the underside, or a way for a view to declare itself deliberately empty so that empty-by-verification counts where empty-by-omission does not

devices.description: Edgecore AGR420 (AS7946-74XKSB) 25GbE aggregation router. 2RU, 74 fixed ports - 2 x 100G QSFP-DD, 8 x 40/100G QSFP28 and 64 x 10/25G SFP28 - with a timing block, 1+1 redundant PSUs and 4+1 redundant fans.

gaps.note: The QSG's Front LEDs section tables every port family and every system lamp with a colour, and for the management jack says only "RJ-45 OOB Port - Left (link), Right (activity)". No colour, and no behaviour. The AGR420 datasheet has no LED section at all, so the QSG is the only source we hold. The two lamps therefore declare what the guide does say - the right lamp blinks for activity, which is the behaviour the same guide gives every other activity lamp on this device - and the left lamp keeps led-rect's generic off/on rather than an invented green-for-link. The AGR400's QSG (AS7946-30XB-QSG-R04) prints the identical sentence, so this is Edgecore's house style for the OOB jack and not a gap in one revision.
gaps.wanted: a NOS LED table, or photographs of the OOB jack with a link up and traffic running

gaps.note: The datasheet states "Power Consumption - Max: 692 W, Typical: 201 W" with no ambient. The QSG for the same SKU states "527 W at 25 C, 723 W at 45 C". Most of that is explained by ambient rather than by disagreement - 527 W at 25 C sits comfortably below the datasheet maximum - but the 45 C figure EXCEEDS the stated maximum by 31 W, and 45 C is the top of this device's own rated operating range (0 to 45 C), so the figure at that ambient should BE the maximum. 692 W is kept as the datasheet's own maximum.
gaps.wanted: an Edgecore statement of what ambient the datasheet's 692 W assumes, or a measurement at 45 C. Note that the QSG's 25 C figure here, 527 W, is identical to the AGR400 datasheet's stated maximum, which may mean one of the four Edgecore figures is a copy error

gaps.note: Searched and absent, which is why this is asserted rather than left to L27 to imply. Both documents we hold - the datasheet and the QSG - rate the AGR PSUs by INPUT only ("DC Input: -40 to -75V, 40 A, per PS"; "AC Input: 100-120 V 12 A or 200-240 V 7.5 A per PS") and state no output wattage anywhere.
